difficulty_reason: The authors compute K-cohomology and codimension-one residues on Severi–Brauer varieties using squarefree-degree K2 and reduced norms, Quillen K-theory, Gersten spectral sequences, and higher Riemann–Roch. They use generic splitting and symbol-length induction for injectivity, then construct a tower preserving the cokernel and killing mod-p K2, prove Brauer vanishing, and pass from prime to arbitrary invertible n.
statement_scope: For every field F and positive integer n invertible in F, the degree-two Galois symbol R_{F,n}: K_2(F)/nK_2(F) → H^2(F,μ_n^{⊗2}) is an isomorphism. The field K_2 is Milnor K_2 by Matsumoto's theorem. The original statement does not require a primitive n-th root in F. Milne IV §5 records its Brauer presentation in the case of a chosen primitive root.

original_book_reference.author: J. S. Milne
original_book_reference.locator: Physical p152 bottom for the generators and p153 before Exercise 5.7 for the Milnor K2 presentation, the isomorphism, and footnote 6 linking to the 1982 Russian original.
original_book_reference.relation: With a primitive n-th root ζ in k, Milne defines i^n=a, j^n=b, ij=ζji and writes {a,b}↦[A(a,b;ζ)] as an isomorphism K_2^M(k)/n→Br(k)[n]. This is the primitive-root Brauer presentation of the original Theorem (11.5), whose target is H^2(k,μ_n⊗μ_n).

cited_symbol_reference.author: John Milnor
cited_symbol_reference.title: Introduction to Algebraic K-Theory
cited_symbol_reference.version: Annals of Mathematics Studies 72, Princeton University Press and University of Tokyo Press, 1971
cited_symbol_reference.locator: §15, printed p143 definition of A_ω(a,b); compare printed p146 displayed product relations. Original article [3], cited in the introduction and §9.
cited_symbol_reference.relation: Milnor uses x^n=a, y^n=b and yx=ωxy. With x=i, y=j and ω=ζ^(-1), this is exactly Milne's ij=ζji. Use ξ=ζ^(-1) in the original paper's primitive-root identification ξ⊗ξ↦ξ. The Kummer sequence then identifies H^2(k,μ_n) with Br(k)[n]. The original paper states this convention for prime p at §9 and writes the arbitrary-n cyclic cup formula [A_ξ(β,a)]=φ_β∪Res χ_a in the proof of (16.3).

source_caveats: The statement and all selected proof pages are from the unchanged official English translation. Its embedded OCR loses some mathematical glyphs, so the scanned page images are authoritative.
The original proof of Theorem (11.5) ends before §12 on printed p328. Later numbered applications, including §16.1 about tensor products of cyclic algebras, are separate from the selected result.

The Milne relationship uses Milnor's presentation A_ω(a,b) with yx=ωxy and Milne's relation ij=ζji. Under x=i and y=j, the compatible primitive root is ω=ζ^{-1}. This is a dictionary of conventions and introduces no new proof of (11.5).
